column2: Here too they cite these collected words of Bodhya, set down on detachment; learn them, Yudhishthira.
King Nahusha questioned the self-controlled sage Bodhya, who had reached peace through detachment, calm, and satisfied with wisdom.
Greatly wise one, give me instruction in peace; thinking on what understanding do you roam calm and content?
[Bodhya said:] "I live by instruction; I teach no one here; I shall tell you its mark; let it be considered by yourself.
Pingala, the osprey, the serpent, the search of the deer in the forest, the arrow-maker, and the maiden: these are my teachers."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Prahlada with the sage who lived like a python.
Prahlada, wise and approved by the wise, king, questioned a certain brahmana roaming, at ease of mind and free of disease.

Healthy, capable, gentle, self-controlled, without contentiousness, free of envy, of good speech, esteemed in the world, wise, you roam like a child.
mahabharata:12:172.5	You do not seek gain nor grieve over loss; ever as if satisfied, brahmana, you slight nothing at all.
mahabharata:12:172.6	While the people are being swept away by the current, you seem undisturbed, unmoved like a mountain peak in the tasks of dharma, desire and wealth.
mahabharata:12:172.7	You do not pursue dharma and wealth, nor do you engage in desire; disregarding the objects of the senses, you roam freed like a witness.
mahabharata:12:172.8	What is your wisdom, sage, what learning, what livelihood? Quickly tell me, brahmana, what you consider the highest good here.
Thus questioned, the wise one, who knew the ordinances of the world's dharma, answered Prahlada with gentle, unharmful speech.

I perceive the end, in turn, even of water-born creatures, of great bodies and of tiny ones in the great ocean.
mahabharata:12:172.15	Of the moving and unmoving beings, lord of the asuras, even of kings, I see death plainly everywhere.
mahabharata:12:172.16	Of sky-roamers also, best of the Danavas, of birds, death rises in due time, even of the powerful.
mahabharata:12:172.17	The lights wandering in heaven, small and great, I see falling in due time.
mahabharata:12:172.18	Seeing thus beings bound by death, equal in all, I, learned and with my duty done, sleep happily.
mahabharata:12:172.19	I swallow even a very large mouthful obtained by chance; I lie again many days without eating.
mahabharata:12:172.20	Food flows to me again, plentiful and of many good qualities; then again little and of few qualities; then again none at all.
mahabharata:12:172.21	Sometimes I eat grains, sometimes oil-cake; I eat rice and meats, and various dishes again.
mahabharata:12:172.22	Sometimes I lie on a couch, sometimes on the ground; sometimes a bed is had even in a palace.
mahabharata:12:172.23	I wear rags, hemp, linen and deerskins; at one time I wear very costly garments.
mahabharata:12:172.24	I neither refuse the righteous enjoyment that comes by chance, nor pursue it when hard to get.
mahabharata:12:172.25	Unmoving, deathless, auspicious, free of grief, pure, unequalled, esteemed by the learned, unliked and unpractised by fools: this python-vow I follow, pure.
mahabharata:12:172.26	With unwavering mind, not falling from my dharma, with limited wandering, knowing high and low, free of fear, passion, greed and delusion, I follow this python-vow, pure.
mahabharata:12:172.27	Eating and drinking food of uncertain kind, with place and time divided by the turn of fate, pleasing to the heart and unpractised by misers, I follow this python-vow, pure.
mahabharata:12:172.28	Seeing people overcome by craving, this, this," losing heart without gaining wealth, I follow, by subtle understanding of truth, this python-vow, pure.
Seeing in many ways the wretched man here, noble or ignoble, resorting to others for the sake of wealth, I, self-possessed, calm, delighting in peace, follow this python-vow, pure.
Seeing in truth that pleasure and pain, harm and gain, delight and disgust, death and life are fixed by ordinance, I follow this python-vow, pure.
Free of fear, passion, delusion and pride, endowed with steadiness, intellect and wisdom, calm, seeing the enjoyers of their fruit arrived, I follow this python-vow, pure.
With uncertain bed and seat by nature, joined with self-control, rules, vows, truth and purity, free of hoarding the fruit, delighted, I follow this python-vow, pure.
Seeing that what comes by efforts for gain brings no happiness, with understanding gained and established in myself, to restrain the thirsty, unsteady mind, I follow this python-vow, pure.
Neither heart nor mind runs after it, seeing the difficulty of getting dear pleasure and its impermanence, both together; I follow this python-vow, pure.
Much has been said of this by the wise, by poets spreading their own fame: "this, this," here and there, searching the depths by their own views.
Having reflected on that, so varied and taken up by unwise men here, unfinished, with endless faults, I roam among men, my anger and craving subdued.
[Bhishma said:] The great-souled man here who follows the way of the python, with attachment tamed, free of fear, anger, greed and delusion, would indeed roam happily in this manner of life."
[Bhishma said:] "Wisdom is the support of beings; wisdom is held to be the highest gain; wisdom is the highest good in the world; wisdom is heaven for the good.
By wisdom Bali, when his lordship was lost, Prahlada, Namuchi and Manki won their ends; what is higher than it?
Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Indra and Kashyapa; learn it, Yudhishthira.
A certain vaishya, proud of his wealth, dear, knocked down with his chariot the sage Kashyapa, of strict vows, an ascetic.
Fallen, in pain and angry, he gave up on himself and said, "I shall die, poor as I am; there is no purpose in living."
As he sat thus wishing to die, silent and senseless, Indra in the form of a jackal appeared to him, his mind angry.

All beings everywhere wish for a human birth, and in human birth all rejoice in brahminhood.
mahabharata:12:173.9	You are a human, a brahmana, and learned in the Veda, Kashyapa; having gained this so hard to gain, you wish to die without fault.
mahabharata:12:173.14	They make protections from snow, rain and heat, and enjoy cloth, food, comfort, bed and shelter from the wind.
mahabharata:12:173.15	Mounting the cow in the world, they enjoy and drive her; by many devices they make others subject to themselves.
mahabharata:12:173.16	Those who are tongueless, wretched, with little breath and no hands endure those sorrows; by good fortune you, sage, are not so.
mahabharata:12:173.17	By good fortune you are not a jackal, nor a worm, nor a mouse, nor a snake, nor a frog, nor any other born of a sinful womb.
mahabharata:12:173.18	Even with this much gain you should be content, Kashyapa; how much more as the best of brahmanas among all beings?
[Kashyapa said:] "These worms eat me; I have no power to take them off, being without hands; see my condition.
And because it is not to be done, I do not give up myself, lest I fall from here into a still more sinful birth."
[The jackal said:] "Among sinful births, I am a jackal, and have gone to it; many other sinful births are worse than this.
Some by birth alone are happier, others are greatly afflicted; I see no one anywhere here who is wholly happy.
Men, having got wealth, wish for kingship next; from kingship they wish for godhood, and from godhood even Indra's rank.
Even if you were rich, neither king nor god, and having gained godhood, even Indrahood, you would not be content so.
There is no satiety in gaining the dear; craving is not quenched by water; it blazes up again, as fire with fuel.
You have grief, and you have joy; and pleasure and pain both; what is the lament there?
Cutting off the roots of all desires and all actions, shut in the host of the senses, like birds in a cage.
Desire is never born in one who does not know tastes; it is born of touch, sight or hearing.
You do not remember liquor, or the lataka birds; and nothing at all is more worth eating than those two.
And whatever other foods and dishes there are far away, Kashyapa, for those who have not eaten them before, there is not even memory.
Not eating, not touching, not seeing: this is the rule for a man, I think, and the good, without doubt.
Men with hands, joined with wealth, strong, without doubt, are made slaves by men themselves.
They are afflicted again and again by killing, binding and distress; and yet they too delight, rejoice and laugh.
Others, strong of arm, learned and high-minded, take up a despised, wretched and sinful livelihood.
They are able to pursue another livelihood too, but it must be fixed by one's own deed, and it is so.
Neither the Pulkasa nor the Chandala wishes to give up himself; see what a delusion, discontent with one's own womb.
Seeing men crippled and struck down, sick, you are, Kashyapa, fully endowed with your own womb, having won a prize.
If your brahmana body is free of fear and of disease, and your limbs are whole, and you are not scorned in the worlds,
not by any slander, only by the truth that carries off, rise up for dharma, brahmana sage; you should not give up yourself.
If, brahmana, you listen to this and have faith in my words, you will gain the chief fruit of the dharma spoken in the Veda.
Carefully keep up study and the tending of the fires, truth, self-control and giving; do not compete with anyone.
Those who have studied their own study and gained sacrifice and officiating, how could they ever grieve or dwell on the unfair?
Wishing for pleasure, they would gain great happiness; those born under a good star, at good bathing-places, at good moments,
while others, born under asura stars, at bad places and bad moments, fall into asura wombs devoid of the birth of sacrifice.
I was once a pedant, a rationalist, a reviler of the Veda, devoted to logic and the science of argument, to no purpose.
A propounder of arguments, a speaker with reasons in assemblies, a reviler and rebuker of the twice-born in sacrifices of Brahman,
an unbeliever, suspicious of all, a fool who thought himself a scholar: this is the result of that, my jackalhood, brahmana.
Might it happen, even after hundreds of days and nights, that I, a jackal, would gain a human womb again?
Content and careful, delighting in sacrifice, giving and austerity, I would be a knower of what is to be known and an avoider of what is to be avoided."
Then the sage Kashyapa rose and said to him, "Oh, how clever you are, how wise!" astonished.
The brahmana looked at him with an eye lengthened by knowledge, and saw him as Indra, the god, lord of the gods, husband of Shachi.
Then Kashyapa honoured the one with bay horses, and, permitted by him, entered his own hermitage.
[Bhishma said:] "The mind, joined with its own harm, enters sin; having done a stained deed, he is set in great affliction.
From famine to famine, from affliction to affliction, from fear to fear; from the dead to the dead go the poor, the doers of sin.
From festival to festival they go, from heaven to heaven, from happiness to happiness: the faithful, the self-controlled, the rich, the doers of good.
In the strongholds of beasts and elephants and the dangers of serpents and thieves, the unbelievers go with a hand-offering; what is higher than this?
Dear to gods and guests, generous, dear to the good, they have taken the path of safety of the self-possessed, with open hand.
Like husks among grains, like putrid insects among birds, such are those among men for whom dharma is no cause.
Even one running very swiftly is followed by ordinance; one lies down with the one who lies down, according to what each has done.
It attends the one who stands, follows the one who goes, acts with the one who acts, like a shadow it follows.
Time drags this host of beings on every side, cast about by the fruit of their own deeds and guarded by ordinance.
As flowers and fruits, unprompted, do not pass their own time, so the deed done before does not.
Honour and dishonour, gain and loss, decay and rise, having proceeded, turn back again and again at the end of ordinance.
Sorrow is made by oneself and pleasure is made by oneself; taking up the bed of the womb, what belongs to a former body is enjoyed.
Child, youth and old man, whatever good or bad he does, in that very state he enjoys it, birth after birth.
As among thousands of cows the calf finds its mother, so a deed done before follows the doer.
A garment soiled in front is cleansed behind by action; for those heated by fasting, long and endless happiness.
By long austerity practised in the penance forest, the desires of those whose sins are shaken off by dharma are accomplished.
As the path of birds in the sky or of fish in water is not seen, so is the course of those who know.
Enough of other reproaches and recited transgressions; what is pleasing and suitable and beneficial to oneself should be done."
[Yudhishthira said:] "This world, with its seas, sky, mountains, clouds, earth, fire and wind: by whom was it made?
How were beings created, how the divisions of class, how purity and impurity, how dharma and adharma?
What is the soul of the living like, and where do the dead go? Tell us all of this, from this world to the other."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, the excellent discourse spoken by Bhrigu to Bharadvaja, who asked.
On the peak of Kailasa, seeing the great sage Bhrigu sitting, as if blazing with energy, Bharadvaja asked him:

This world, with its seas, sky, mountains, clouds, earth, fire and wind: by whom was it made?
mahabharata:12:175.8	How were beings created, how the divisions of class, how purity and impurity, how dharma and adharma?
mahabharata:12:175.9	What is the soul of the living like, and where do the dead go? Tell us all of the other world too, blessed one.
Known as the Mental, heard of before by great sages, the god without beginning or end, unsplittable, unageing and immortal,
called the Unmanifest, eternal, imperishable, undecaying, from whom beings are created, born and die.
That god first created the one called the Great, known as Space, the lord who bears all beings.
From space came water; from water, fire and wind; from the union of fire and wind then came the earth.
Then the self-born made a divine lotus full of splendour; from that lotus was born Brahma, the Veda-formed treasure.
Called Ego, the maker of the self of all beings, Brahma of great splendour is he who is these five elements.
The mountains are called his bones; the earth is his fat and flesh; the oceans are his blood; space is his belly.
Wind is his breath, fire his heat, the rivers his veins; fire and Soma, the moon and sun, are known as his eyes.
The sky above is his head, the earth his feet, the directions his arms; he is hard to know from his endlessness, even for the perfected, without doubt.
He himself is the blessed Vishnu, known as Endless, dwelling as the self of all beings, hard for the unrefined to know.
He is the creator of ego for the origin of all beings, from whom the universe arose, as you have asked me here."
[Bharadvaja said:] "What are the measures here of the sky, the directions, the earth and the wind? Cut my doubt according to the truth."
[Bhrigu said:] "This space is endless, frequented by perfected beings and charanas, lovely, crowded with many abodes, whose end cannot be reached.
Above the path of motion and below it, the moon and sun are not seen; there the gods shine of themselves, radiant, with the lustre of fire.
Even they, famed for power, do not see the end of the sky, because of its being hard to reach and endless; know this, giver of honour.
Layer upon layer, this space is closed in by self-luminous blazing ones, immeasurable even by the gods.
At the end of the earth are the oceans; at the end of the oceans, darkness is said to be; at the end of darkness they say is water; at the end of water, fire.
At the end of the nether world is water; at the end of water the lord of serpents; at his end again space; at the end of space again water.
Thus the measure of the blessed one and of water has an end, hard to know even for the gods, by fire, wind and water.
The colours of fire, wind, water and the surface of the earth are like space; they are distinguished by the vision of truth.
Sages also recite in various scriptures how the measure is laid down in the three worlds and the ocean; who could state the measure of the unseen and unreachable?
When the course of the perfected and the gods is limited, then the name 'Endless' is figurative; the great-souled Mental has a name fitting his nature.
When that divine form shrinks and grows again, who else is able to know it, or who like him?
Then from the lotus was created the omniscient, embodied lord Brahma, made of dharma, the first and unsurpassed Prajapati."
[Bharadvaja said:] "If he was born of the lotus, the lotus is elder; yet you call Brahma the first-born; I have doubt."
[Bhrigu said:] "The form of the Mental which attained Brahma-hood: for his seat the earth is called a lotus.
The pericarp of that lotus is Meru, rising to the sky; standing in its midst, the lord creates the worlds."
[Bhrigu said:] "The Mental created by mind the manifold creation of beings; first he made water, for kindling beings.
That by which the life of all beings grows and by which subjects thrive, and which, abandoned, they perish: by it all this is covered.
The earth, the mountains, the clouds and whatever else has form, all that is to be known as of Varuna; the waters held them up again."
[Bharadvaja said:] "How did water arise, and fire and wind, and how was the earth created? Here I have great doubt."
[Bhrigu said:] "In the Brahma-kalpa of old, brahmana, at a gathering of the Brahmarshis, doubt about the origin of the world arose among the great souls.
They stood in meditation, taking up silence, motionless, giving up food and living on air, for a divine hundred years, twice-born.
Then to all of them a voice full of dharma came to the ear; divine Sarasvati arose there from the sky.

Formerly the sky, still and soundless, like a mountain unmoving, without moon, sun or wind, shone as if asleep.
mahabharata:12:176.11	As a vessel without a hole seems silent, and when filled with water the wind makes it sound,
mahabharata:12:176.12	so, when the sky was blocked with water at its end, without gaps, the wind, splitting the bottom of the ocean, rose up with a roar.
mahabharata:12:176.13	This wind moves, born of the ocean's pressure, and reaching the place of space, does not find rest.
mahabharata:12:176.14	In the clash of wind and water, a blazing, mighty fire appears with its flame upward, making the sky free of darkness.
mahabharata:12:176.15	Fire joined with wind rises from the sky as water; by the union of fire and wind it attains solidity.
mahabharata:12:176.16	Whatever oil of it fell in space and stayed became aggregated and turned into earth.
mahabharata:12:176.17	Earth is to be known here as the womb of tastes, all scents, oils and living beings, from which everything is born.
[Bharadvaja said:] "Of the thousands of beings the wise one created, how is it that only five come to be elements?"
[Bhrigu said:] "Beings of immeasurable number come to origin; therefore the great word 'elements' applies to them.
Movement is wind, hollow is space, heat is fire, fluid is water, and earth is the compound; the body is made of the five elements.
So the moving and unmoving are joined with these five elements; hearing, smell, taste, touch and sight are called the senses."
[Bharadvaja said:] "If moving and unmoving are joined with five elements, the five constituents are not seen in the bodies of the unmoving.
In trees, which are without warmth, without movement and dense, truly, the five constituents are not found in the body.
They do not hear, do not see, do not know scent or taste, and do not know touch; how are they made of five elements?
Because of lack of fluidity, lack of fire, lack of earth, lack of wind, and the immeasurability of space, there is no element in trees."
[Bhrigu said:] "Fruit and flower fall away from wind, fire and the thunderbolt's blow; sound is grasped by hearing, and so trees hear.
A creeper winds round a tree and goes everywhere; there is no path for the unseeing; so trees see.
By holy and unholy scents and by various incenses, trees become healthy and flower; so trees smell.
They drink water with their feet, and are seen to have disease and cure for disease; so a tree has taste.
As one draws water upward through the stalk of a lotus with the mouth, so trees, joined with wind, drink with their feet.
From the experience of pleasure and pain, and growth when cut, I see life in trees; they are not without consciousness.
The water taken in by them is digested by fire and wind; and from the transformation of food comes oil and growth.
In the bodies of all moving beings the five constituents are distinguished one by one, by which the body acts.
Skin, flesh, bones, marrow and sinew as the fifth: this is counted here as the earthy part of the body.
Energy, fire, anger, the eye and heat; and fire digests also; embodied beings are made of five fiery parts.
Hearing, smell, the mouth, the heart and the belly: these five constituents in the body of living beings are from space.
Phlegm, bile, sweat, fat and blood: so water in the body of living beings is always fivefold.
The living being breathes by prana, extends by vyana, apana goes downward, and samana abides in the heart.
By udana he breathes upward and speaks by its divisions; these five winds move the embodied one here.
The embodied one knows the quality of smell from earth, taste from water, sees light with the eyes, and knows touch by wind.
Of that smell I shall tell the qualities in detail: pleasant and unpleasant smell, sweet and sharp,
spreading, compact, oily, rough and clear: so the extent of earthy smell is to be known as ninefold.
Sound, touch, form and taste are held to be the qualities of water; I shall tell the knowledge of taste; hear it as I tell.
Taste is said by the wise of renowned minds to be of many kinds: sweet, salt, bitter, astringent, sour and pungent; this sixfold taste is held to be made of water.
Sound, touch and form: light is said to have three qualities; light sees forms, and form is held to be of many kinds.
Short, long, thick, square, round, white, black, red, blue, yellow and ruddy: so light's form is held to have twelve varieties.
Sound and touch are to be known; wind is said to have two qualities; the quality of wind is touch, and touch is held to be of many kinds.
Hard, smooth, slick, sticky, soft, harsh, hot, cold, pleasant, painful, oily and clear: so the quality of wind is declared to have twelve varieties.
Space has one quality, which is held to be sound; I shall tell of that sound in its manifold variety.
Shadja, rishabha, gandhara, madhyama and panchama, and dhaivata, and likewise nishada.
This is called the sevenfold quality marked by space; it stays everywhere in threefold voice, even in drums and the like.
They say sound is born of space; with these qualities of wind it perceives; it does not know when they come in disorder.
And these constituents are ever nourished by those constituents; water, fire and wind are ever awake in embodied beings."
[Bhrigu said:] "I shall tell you, brahmana, sinless one, the movement of the wind, how the mighty wind moves the bodies of living beings.
Fire, resting on the head and protecting the body, and prana, abiding in the head and in the fire, set the body in motion.
The creature, the self of all beings, is the eternal Person; mind, intellect, ego, the elements and the objects are he.
So here he is protected everywhere by prana, and behind by samana, each resting on its own course.
Resting in the root of the bladder and the anus and in the fire, apana circulates, carrying urine and excrement.
That which, in effort, action and strength, abides in the three is called udana by those who know the self.
The wind that is present in all the joints of men's bodies is taught as vyana.
Fire spreads in the constituents, stirred by samana, and stays, setting going the juices, constituents and humours.
From the meeting of the breaths a meeting arises; heat is to be known as the fire that digests food in embodied beings.
Prana, carrying the force of fire, is struck at the end of the anus, and rising again throws up the fire.
The place of digested food is below the navel, the stomach above; in the middle of the navel all the breaths of the body are gathered.
Spreading from the heart, all go crosswise, upward and downward; ten breaths, urged on, carry the juices of food.
The son of Dasha ashva was a most righteous king, whose mind was ever devoted to truth, austerity and giving.
Where does that wealth now remain, blessed one, and how can we obtain it, rich in austerity?
I who did not find you, king, in pain and thin from fasting, living on restrained food and lying on the ground, with my brothers,
Then the Andhakas, Bhojas, Shaineyas and Vrishnis, driven by time, struck one another in the tumult with clubs.
[Dharma said:] "Because you gave up even a divine chariot saying, 'This dog is a devotee,' there is no one equal to you in heaven, lord of men."
The Maruts with Shakra, the Vasus and the Ashvins, the Sadhyas, Rudras and Adityas, and the other dwellers of heaven.
